false_assumption.statement: Harvey Grimm was the thief who stole Madame de Borria's necklace.
false_assumption.why_it_seems_reasonable: Grimm was found in possession of a necklace similar to the stolen one and was caught with tools for cutting jewels, making him appear guilty. The police and detective Brodie strongly suspected him.
false_assumption.what_it_hides: The necklace Grimm had was entrusted to him for secret disposal by the rightful owners, the Brinnen family, who pretended to be criminals to protect the jewels. Grimm was acting under their instructions, not as a thief.

mechanism_description: Harvey Grimm, under the alias Ed. Levy, acted as the skilled artisan who secretly recut and disguised the stolen jewels to prevent their identification. The Brinnen family pretended to be criminals to protect the true ownership of the jewels, using the theft narrative as a cover. Grimm cleverly concealed the genuine necklace separate from the fake one to mislead the police and orchestrated the recovery and sale of the jewels while evading capture.

discriminating_test.design: The test involves verifying the presence and handling of the real necklace versus the fake one in controlled environments, including police custody and hotel rooms. By tracking the necklace's location and comparing it with suspects' movements and alibis, the investigators can prove who had access to the genuine jewels and who only possessed replicas.
discriminating_test.knowledge_revealed: This test reveals that Harvey Grimm was entrusted with the real necklace and only possessed the fake one when confronted by the police, proving his role as a protector rather than a thief.
discriminating_test.pass_condition: The real necklace is found in Grimm's possession separate from the fake one held by the police, confirming his innocence of theft and his role in the secret disposal.
